hybrid electric aircraft energy management strategy

abstract
Hybrid electric aircraft concepts are high in future aviation agenda to enabling reduced fuel consumption
and emissions. However, the additional weight of the introduced battery and electrical components and
sizing cascading effects will impact aircraft mission analysis performance. Therefore, the potential
beneﬁt of adopting hybrid electric aircraft will highly depend on the applied energy management
strategy (EMS). This paper presents a three-layer propulsion-mission analysis-EMS integrated multi-
objective optimization scheme for hybrid electric aircraft identifying feasible design aspects consid-
ering fully coupled propulsion-aerodynamics effects. The ‘propulsion’ layer comprises the propulsion
system modelling, integration approaches, and performance synthesis using an Arti ﬁcial Neural Network
(ANN)-based gas turbine surrogate model. The ‘mission-analysis’ layer is designed for multi-energy
sources hybrid electric aircraft mission analysis considering fully coupled propulsion-aerodynamic ef-
fects. The ‘EMS’ layer utilizes non-dominated sorting genetic algorithm II (NSGA-II) addressing the design
trade-off, i.e., block fuel burn, energy consumption, emissions. The proposed scheme is applied to a
typical narrow-body aircraft, Boeing 737 e800, equipped with mechanically integrated hybrid electric
parallel propulsion con ﬁguration to explore ﬂight electri ﬁcation in civil aviation. Moreover, sensitivity
analysis of battery technology level and ﬂight mission de ﬁnition is followed providing insights to hybrid
electric aircraft application scenarios. The EMS optimization results indicate that for short/medium haul
aircrafts which operate in high altitude with long ﬂight durations, fuel as consumable energy source is
prone to be used in initial stages to reduce aircraft weight and lift-dependent drag, while battery as non-
consumable energy is optimally allocated in ﬁnal ﬂight stages of descent and landing. The design of
hybrid electric aircraft is highly sensitive to both ﬂight mission de ﬁnition and battery speci ﬁc energy
projections. With battery speci ﬁc energy projections of 1500 Wh/kg for the year 2035, optimal block fuel
burn reduction by /C0 44.62%, /C0 31.47% and /C0 21.86% can be obtained at the ﬂight range design of 1000 nmi,
1250 nmi and 1500 nmi respectively.

1. Introduction
The global aircraft ﬂeet consumed over 7% of oil products (276
million tons of jet fuel) and produced 2.7% of energy-consumption
related CO2 emissions due to in- ﬂight combustion [ 1]. Considering
that global aviation demand is anticipated to grow at around 4.8%
annually, it is critical to reduce the environmental footprint of the
aviation industry [ 2]. Different organization and research councils
have published pathways for reducing aviation related pollutant
emissions. For example, NASA ‘Nþ3’ aims for /C0 75% NOx
emissions, /C0 70% fuel burn and /C0 55 dB noise at the airport
boundary in the year of 2035 [ 3]. However, the potential ef ﬁciency
improvements from conventional technologies progress in
airframe, structure, propulsion, and air-traf ﬁc management are
already reaching a plateau [ 4]. Thus, it is unlikely to achieve these
ambitious goals through conventional technologies. Electric pro-
pulsion in aviation has emerged as a feasible solution to facilitate
the environmental impacts supported by the recent progress in
battery technology. Batteries can provide electrical power without
direct combustion emissions, and these emissions can be alleviated
effectively on the ground-based power plants, with feasible inte-

and wave for the generation of electric power [ 5]. Additionally,
electric propulsion decouples the gas turbine from propulsors and
removes assembly constraints by using electrical connections,
which has the potential to improve the overall propulsion system
efﬁciency by operating fans and gas turbines at their maximum
efﬁciency [ 4], while electrochemical storage systems have higher
energy conversion ef ﬁciency compared to thermal ones.
However, electric propulsion development is highly dependent
on electrical components and battery technology advancement. For
instance, battery speci ﬁc energy is projected to achieve 1500 Wh/
kg in the year 2035þ [6], but even then, it will contain just 12.30% of
the energy content per unit weight of jet fuel (43.9 MJ/kg). Thus, as
an energy source, the battery demonstrates very low energy den-
sity, signi ﬁcantly increasing the weight of energy stored onboard
and leading to higher drag. Batteries would also not lose mass in-
ﬂight, further penalizing their aviation application. Apart from
energy storage, electric machines, power electronics, transmission
and thermal management components needed for an electrical
propulsion system also increase aircraft take-off gross weight, thus,
a fully electric battery-powered con ﬁguration is not seen as a vital
solution for commercial aviation [ 7]. For regional and single-aisle
aircraft, hybrid-electric aircraft would be a feasible solution to
make more use of electrical energy from a battery that reduces fuel
burn and emissions as well as increasing the lifetime of gas turbine.
Considering the state-of-the-art and projections for electric ma-
chines and battery technology will enable the adoption of hybrid-
electric aircraft for medium-haul routes. Our study focuses on
single-aisle hybrid electric propulsion aircraft systems [ 8].
The EMS for hybrid electric aircraft is a challenge. Firstly, the gas
turbine fuel ﬂow rate in- ﬂight signiﬁcantly impacts aircraft weight
during ﬂight mission, which further affects lift-dependent drag and
thrust demand. Although the introduction of an electrical power-
train would improve fuel consumption and emissions performance
at the propulsion system level, it might deteriorate the integrated
aircraft performance due to the drag penalty. For assessing hybrid
electric aircraft propulsion systems, ﬂight segment weight change
and energy balance should be considered in the mission analysis. In
this context, onboard energy should be equal to mission energy
demand for a de ﬁned ﬂight mission, as an excessive amount of
energy onboard would induce weight and drag penalty. This is
signiﬁcantly different from ground hybrid electric vehicles, given
that EMS of hybrid electric aircraft explores optimum hybridization
of power at each mission segment from a global optimization
perspective at an integrated aircraft level. A fully coupled
propulsion-aerodynamics-weight multidisciplinary model, with
suitable ﬁdelity, is required for the EMS optimization.
Existing research work on hybrid electric propulsion systems is
focused on preliminary sizing and mission analysis. Sliwinski et al.
[9] developed a hybrid electric propulsion system retro ﬁt design
methodology for unmanned aircraft with internal combustion and
electric propulsion combination to improve endurance or ﬂight
range performance. However, the internal combustion engine
performance is modelled as constant speci ﬁc fuel consumption in
this study. This is different from a gas turbine utilized in narrow-
body or single-aisle aircraft whose gas turbine is highly sensitive
to ﬂight conditions. Sziroczak et al. [ 10] developed a conceptual
design process for small electric and hybrid-electric aircraft with an
internal combustion engine using energy fractions approach to
achieve ﬂight segment weight and energy balance through itera-
tion, but propeller and internal combustion engine operating ef ﬁ-
ciency is only estimated by performance maps with no
consideration of ﬂight conditions. This methodology is also
employed to assess small aircraft energy consumption performance
in Ref. [ 11]. Donateo et al. [ 12] proposed a novel approach of
assessing ﬂight endurance of electric ﬂight to compare fuel cell-
powered and battery-powered aircraft. However, batteries as
non-consumable energy sources do not change the aircraft weight
and lift-dependent drag during the ﬂight missions, which should be
considered in fuel-powered aircraft and hybrid electric aircraft. In
Ref. [ 13], Finger et al. proposed a preliminary sizing methodology
for hybrid electric general aviation aircraft based on point perfor-
mance constraints and mission performance speci ﬁcation. How-
ever, this study holds engine speci ﬁc power and ef ﬁciency as a
constant value instead of a detailed gas turbine off-design perfor-
mance model. In addition, this study does not account for gas
turbine-electrical powertrain coupling effects. To reduce compu-
tational complexity and simultaneously ensure model accuracy, De
Vries et al. [ 14] initially developed a methodology for hybrid elec-
tric aircraft conceptual design by generating multidimensional ta-
bles of gas turbine and propulsive device characteristics
independent of the aircraft design environment, then interpolation
methods are used to calculate gas turbine and propulsive device
characteristics within preliminary aircraft sizing process.
EMS is to facilitate the coordinated operation of gas turbine and
electrical powertrain to obtain optimal performance on fuel burn,
energy consumption, and emissions considering interactions be-
tween propulsion, weight, and aerodynamics. Carlo [ 15] proposed
energy-optimal off-design power management for a light, single-
propeller hybrid electric motor glider, with limited energy avail-
ability on-board. Pornet et al. [ 16] developed an energy manage-
ment optimization process that is simpli ﬁed and performed by
considering a ﬁxed power split factor between dual-energy sources
(fuel and electrical energy) for climb and cruise segments. The
increased mass of the electrical powertrain and battery is accom-
modated by reducing payload and ﬂight range. In Ref. [ 17], Ang
et al. performed the EMS by looping for power-split in take-off and
climb phases and optimizing and scaling down gas turbine for
cruise condition for a hybrid turbofan engine powered A320 aircraft
on a short-range ﬂight mission. Furthermore, Donateo et al. [ 18]
applied dynamic programming to obtain optimal power-split se-
quences. Teresa et al. [ 19] proposed an energy management strat-
egy in a hybrid electric helicopter for urban air mobility to obtain
the optimal usage of dual-energy sources using dynamic pro-
gramming for of
ﬂine optimization and equivalent consumption
minimization strategy for online optimization. However, these
studies are proposed based on the prior-known power demand
proﬁles. They only investigated isolated propulsion system per-
formance; aero-propulsive coupling effects are not considered. Ye
et al. [ 20] proposed a fuzzy logic-based equivalent consumption
optimization for hybrid electric unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs).
However, different from commercial aircraft, UAVs operate at low
altitudes with short ﬂight durations using an internal combustion
engine. The performance of UAVs is not sensitive to ﬂight condi-
tions, energy balance, and weight-induced drag penalty will also
not be a concern for lightweight UAVs. In Ref. [ 21], Zamboni et al.
conducted a single objective optimization process with a mono-
lithic architecture based on isolated gas turbine and aircraft
mission analysis models, then manual iteration is performed be-
tween disciplines to ﬁnalize the mission analysis procedure. This
also leaves design space for further optimization of EMS for hybrid
electric aircraft performance. Therefore, a fully coupled propulsion-
aerodynamic multidisciplinary optimization model is essential to
assess and improve hybrid electric aircraft bene ﬁts with improved
accuracy and computational ef ﬁciency.
This paper proposes a multi-objective optimization framework
for optimum energy utilization for mission analysis level to
enhance the performance of hybrid electric propulsion systems
with alternative electrical energy sources. This framework com-
prises gas turbine performance assessment module, electrical
powertrain sizing, and performance assessment module, hybrid

electric mission analysis module, and optimization algorithm
module. Based on novel propulsion con ﬁguration and hybrid en-
ergy sources, the proposed framework can provide performance
evaluation on fuel burn, energy consumption, emissions, and eco-
nomic costs at a de ﬁned battery technology level. Feasible archi-
tecture and energy sources solutions are identi ﬁed for design
purposes with applications on general aviation, regional aviation,
and narrow-body aircraft.
The main contributions of this paper are summarized as follows:
1) This paper innovatively establishes a high- ﬁdelity ANN-based
gas turbine surrogate model based on Levenberg-Marquardt
back-propagation algorithm to evaluate the gas turbine perfor-
mance. The ANN-based gas turbine surrogate model speci ﬁcally
considers the gas turbine components rematching and calcu-
lates the effect of operating point change due to electri ﬁcation
on engine performance and combustor inlet conditions. The
proposed model can simultaneously reduce computational ef-
forts and time for mission analysis and optimization procedures.
2) A methodology of mission analysis is developed for hybrid
electric aircraft by considering aerodynamics, maneuver
requirement, weight property, propulsion system characteris-
tics, electrical powertrain sizing, and performance to ﬁnd a so-
lution of energy balance based on Newton Raphson method.
3) A fully coupled propulsion-aerodynamic optimization frame-
work is developed based on the proposed hybrid electric aircraft
mission analysis method to assess the optimal trade-off be-
tween optimization objectives including block fuel burn, energy
consumption, and emissions using NSGA-II.
The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. Section II
presents the proposed fully coupled propulsion-aerodynamic
optimization framework and Section III introduces hybrid electric
propulsion con ﬁgurations and modelling and proposes perfor-
mance assessment method for hybrid electric architecture. Espe-
cially, an ANN gas turbine surrogate performance model is
established, which will be used in optimization procedures to
reduce the computational burden. Section IV develops a method-
ology for hybrid electric aircraft mission analysis which takes both
consumable (fuel) and non-consumable (battery) energy sources
into account. Section V proposes a propulsion-mission analysis-
EMS integration multi-objective optimization framework for
hybrid electric aircraft using NSGA-II algorithm. In Section VI, block
fuel burn, energy consumption, and emissions performance of
selected novel propulsion con ﬁguration are discussed and
compared for applications on narrow-body aircraft of Boeing
737e800. Finally, the conclusions are summarized in Section VII.
2. Propulsion-mission analysis-EMS integrated multi-
objective optimization framework
A propulsion-mission analysis-EMS integrated multi-objective
optimization scheme is proposed to obtain optimal propulsion
system performance at integrated aircraft level as shown in Fig. 1.
The ‘propulsion’ layer comprises the propulsion system modelling,
integration approaches, and performance synthesis using an Arti-
ﬁcial Neural Network (ANN)-based gas turbine surrogate model.
The ‘mission-analysis’ layer is designed for multi-energy sources
hybrid electric aircraft mission analysis considering fully coupled
propulsion-aerodynamic effects. The ‘EMS’ layer utilizes non-
dominated sorting genetic algorithm II (NSGA-II) addressing the
design trade-off, i.e., block fuel burn, energy consumption, emis-
sions. The following sections will introduce each layer respectively.
3. Hybrid electric propulsion system modeling and
integration
In this section, the system modelling for mechanically inte-
grated parallel hybrid propulsion con ﬁguration (MIPH) is
described. As shown in Fig. 2
, MIPH consists of turbofan engine,
battery stack, electric machine, power converters, and electric bus.
For MIPH conﬁguration, the battery-powered motor is mounted on
the low-pressure shaft of gas turbine to drive the ducted fan.
Electrical power is directly fed to the drive train of the propulsive
device. The case examined herein is the B737- 800 utilizing two
hybridized CFM56 turbofan engines.

4. Methodology of hybrid electric aircraft mission analysis
In this section, an integrated mission analysis method for hybrid
electric aircraft to evaluate novel propulsion con ﬁguration at
aircraft level is proposed. Herein, an open-source credible con-
ceptual level aircraft design platform, SUAVE, is used and extended
for mission analysis of hybrid electric aircraft with advanced pro-
pulsion technologies. SUAVE provides a set of multidisciplinary
analytical and semi-empirical models for aerodynamics, structures,
conventional propulsion, and stability that allow augmenting

The ﬂow chart of hybrid electric mission analysis is shown in
Fig. 4 . Aircraft mission analysis performs an iterative process for
obtaining a solution of energy balance: required energy versus
energy carried onboard for a speci ﬁc ﬂight mission. The ﬂight

segments. Based on the energy-based approach, the amount of
both consumable energy and non-consumable energy depleted in
each segment are calculated and summed up to estimate the ﬂight
mission fuel and battery mass. The iterative process is converged
when the mission energy balance is satis ﬁed.

6.3. Hybrid electric aircraft EMS optimization
As discussed, performance is not enhanced when a constant

in the literature. Such simple energy management strategies, such
as assuming a constant power split parameter [ 41,42] or a constant
power setting level [ 43,44] does not allow the exploitation of the
ﬂexibility that hybrid propulsion offers. Thus, a computationally
efﬁcient optimization procedure is required to further investigate
optimal EMS from a global optimization perspective at the inte-
grated aircraft level. For assessing the bene ﬁts that an optimized
EMS can offer the proposed optimization algorithm is applied in the
following. The NSGA-II optimization algorithm is applied to the test
case conﬁguration for minimizing block fuel burn and total energy
consumption for dual-engine-electric. As seen in Fig. 8 (a), different
EMS selection will result in different optimal performance of fuel

consumption reduction, highlighting the importance of EMS. It is

7. Discussions
In this section, the proposed mission analysis method is applied
to Boeing 737 e800 with a ﬁxed hybridization of power during
whole ﬂight mission to evaluate parallel hybrid electric propulsion
conﬁguration at integrated aircraft level. It can be concluded that
for the performance of fuel burn reduction, battery speci ﬁc energy
of around 1250 Wh/kg becomes a critical sizing criterion for ﬂight
range of 2000 nmi (3704 km), below of which no signi ﬁcant ben-
eﬁts on block fuel burn reduction can be observed. For low battery
speciﬁc energy assumption, fuel burn reduction bene ﬁts degrade
with higher level of hybridization of power. NOx emissions are
affected by both sides of gas turbine operation (T3 and P3) and
block fuel burn. With high level of hybridization of power, the
beneﬁt of gas turbine power on-take, and reduced block fuel burn
are not capable of offsetting the sizing related drag penalty and
highly increased thrust demand.
For a dynamic hybridization of power strategy, multi-objective
optimization using NSGA-II is adopted to establish an optimal
EMS to minimize block fuel burn and energy consumption for ﬂight
range of 2000 nmi (3704 km). The EMS is applied to different
battery speci ﬁc energy scenarios for sensitivity analysis of battery
technology level. Optimal block fuel reduction of /C0 8.17%, /C0 18.85%
and /C0 29.17% can be achieved at battery speciﬁc energy of 1500 Wh/
kg, 2000 Wh/kg and 2500 Wh/kg for dual-engine-electric opera-
tion, with increased energy consumption penalty of þ8.5%, þ7.9%
and þ6.25% respectively. A trend can be observed that fuel as
consumable energy source is prone to be used in initial stages to
reduce aircraft weight and lift-dependent drag, while battery as
non-consumable energy is optimally allocated in ﬁnal ﬂight stages
of descent and landing.
Sensitivity analysis of ﬂight mission range is performed based
on battery speci ﬁc energy projections of 1500 Wh/kg. Optimal
block fuel burn reduction from /C0 44.62% and /C0 21.86% can be ob-
tained at ﬂight range of 1000 nmi (1852 km) and 1500 nmi
(3704 km) respectively for dual-engine-electric. At ﬂight range of
1000 nmi (1852 km), optimal energy consumption reduction
of /C0 5% can be expected with fuel burn reduction of /C0 26.71%. Po-
tential beneﬁts of block fuel burn reduction and energy consump-
tion reduction degrade with the increased ﬂight range. When ﬂight
range exceeds 2000 nmi (3704 km), no bene ﬁts on energy con-
sumption can be observed and maximum fuel burn reduction is less
than /C0 10%. Sensitivity analysis results of fuel burn reduction, CO2
emissions reduction change signi ﬁcantly for different sets of ﬂight
ranges and battery speci ﬁc energy levels even for the same aircraft
model. Thus, the design of hybrid electric aircraft is highly sensitive
to both ﬂight mission de ﬁnition and battery technology level.
8. Conclusion
This paper proposed an optimization framework for hybrid
electric aircrafts. The particular aspect was to assess and improve
block fuel burn, energy consumption and emissions performance
considering the propulsion-aerodynamics coupled effect. Firstly, an
ANN gas turbine surrogate performance model was established and
integrated with the EMS optimization procedure to ensure
computational ef ﬁciency and high ﬁdelity. The electrical power-
train weight and ef ﬁciency were established upon physics-based
models. Then, mission analysis approach is developed to accom-
modate electrical powertrain and battery energy storage by dis-
cretizing the ﬂight mission segment. Ultimately, an NSGA-II based
multi-objective optimization algorithm is utilized to identify opti-
mized hybridization of power in individual ﬂight phase (i.e.,
minimizing block fuel burn and energy consumption). NOx emis-
sions performance is assessed by using a semi-empirical correla-
tions approach of ‘P3T3’ method, while CO
2 emissions comprise
both in-ﬂight and power grid through carbon emissions index. The
EMS optimization results indicate that fuel as consumable energy
source is prone to be used in initial stages to reduce aircraft weight
and lift-dependent drag, while battery as non-consumable energy
is optimally allocated in ﬁnal ﬂight stages of descent and landing.
Sensitivity analysis results of fuel burn reduction, CO 2/NOx emis-
sions reduction will change signi ﬁcantly for different sets of ﬂight
ranges and battery speci ﬁc energy level. As a result, the design of
hybrid electric aircraft is highly sensitive to both ﬂight mission
deﬁnition design and battery speci ﬁc energy projections. The
beneﬁts of short-range ﬂight mission on block fuel burn, energy
consumption and emissions are superior to that of long-ﬂight range
missions. In terms of emissions performance, both CO 2/NOx emis-
sions show a convex curve relationship between block fuel burn
reduction and emission reduction due to sizing cascading effects.
